slides.title: Skandamata, the mother with Kartik on her lap
slides.sub: The fifth form of Durga, worshipped on Panchami

slides.title: Mother of the gods' commander
slides.body: The mother of Skanda, also called Kartikeya or Murugan. She holds her infant son on her lap and is worshipped as the loving, protective mother.

slides.title: Look beside Durga in any pandal
slides.body: In Bengal, Kartik stands at Durga's side in every pandal idol, a reminder of this bond. She has four arms, two holding lotuses, and sits on a lotus or rides a lion.

slides.text:
सिंहासनगता नित्यं पद्माश्रितकरद्वया ।
शुभदास्तु सदा देवी स्कन्दमाता यशस्विनी ॥
slides.translit: Simhasanagata nityam padmashrita karadvaya, shubhadastu sada devi skandamata yashasvini
slides.meaning: May the glorious Skandamata, ever seated on her lion throne with lotuses in her two hands, always bring what is good.

slides.kicker: Panchami · The story behind the date
slides.title: Why is Durga Puja in autumn, not spring?
slides.sub: Rama's untimely puja, as Krittibas told it

slides.title: Akal bodhon, word by word
slides.body: Akal means untimely, out of season. Bodhon means awakening. Autumn falls in the half of the year counted as the gods' night, when they sleep, so a goddess worshipped now must first be woken.

slides.title: Krittibas, not Valmiki
slides.body: The story is best known from Krittibas Ojha's Bengali Ramayana, usually dated to around the 15th century. In Valmiki's Ramayana, Rama is taught the Aditya Hridayam, a hymn to the sun, instead.

slides.title: Rama wakes the goddess
slides.body: The war in Lanka is going badly, and Rama is advised to win the goddess to his side. On the sixth lunar day he performs the bodhon at the foot of a bel tree and begins the puja.

slides.title: 108 blue lotuses, one missing
slides.body: Hanuman brings 108 blue lotuses. Rama counts 107: the goddess has hidden one to test him. Called lotus-eyed, he raises an arrow to offer his own eye. She stops his hand and blesses him.

slides.title: Basanti Puja kept the spring
slides.body: Tradition places Durga's original worship in spring, in Chaitra, as Basanti Puja. The untimely autumn puja became Bengal's far bigger festival, but some old families and temples still hold Basanti Puja.

slides.title: Still done on Shashthi evening
slides.body: On Shashthi, Saturday 17 October 2026, the priest performs the bodhon, amantran and adhivas at a bel tree or bel branch. The time depends on the tithi: check your local panjika or the puja committee's notice.

slides.title: The puja that began out of season
slides.ask: Send it to someone who asks why

caption.en:
Durga Puja 2026: why is Kolkata's Durga Puja in autumn? The story of akal bodhon 🪔

Akal means untimely, bodhon means awakening. In Krittibas Ojha's Bengali Ramayana, Rama wakes the goddess out of season, at a bel tree, before his last battle with Ravana. The episode is not in Valmiki's Ramayana.

He needs 108 blue lotuses. One goes missing, hidden by the goddess herself to test him, and Rama, the lotus-eyed, raises an arrow to offer his own eye instead. She stops him and promises him victory.

The spring worship never went away: it survives as Basanti Puja. And the bodhon is still done on Shashthi evening, Saturday 17 October this year.

slides.title: Shooting pandals at night on your phone
slides.sub: Expose for her face, skip the flash, ask first

slides.title: Tap on the goddess's face
slides.body: Pandals mix spotlights, coloured LEDs and deep shadow. Tap on her face to expose for it, then pull the exposure down a little so the gold ornaments and white faces keep their detail.

slides.title: Night mode, not flash
slides.body: Use your phone's night mode. A little noise is better than motion blur from people jostling around you. Avoid flash during puja and aarti everywhere; it distracts worshippers and rarely helps.

slides.title: Brace yourself
slides.body: Lean on a barricade or pillar, tuck your elbows in and breathe out as you shoot. Tripods are rarely practical, and often not allowed, in crowded pandals. Shoot RAW if your phone supports it.

slides.title: Use the 2x or 3x lens
slides.body: From the front of the viewing area, a short zoom isolates the face from the crowd. Make sure focus lands on the eyes, then step back for a wide shot of the whole family in the chala.

slides.title: Smoke, embers, movement
slides.body: Dhunuchi naach usually comes at the evening aarti, especially Ashtami and Navami. Use continuous shooting to freeze it, or a slower shutter for the smoke. Keep your distance: dhunuchis are hot and swung fast.

slides.title: Ask before you shoot people
slides.body: Ask before photographing priests, women at prayer, children or anyone during a ritual. Some family pujas restrict photos. Take your shot and step aside; never block the aarti, anjali or a queue.

slides.title: Save this for your pandal nights

caption.en:
How to photograph Kolkata Durga Puja pandals at night on a phone 📸

Tap on the goddess's face. That's where you expose. Then pull the exposure down a little so the gold keeps its detail. Use night mode, brace against a pillar and skip the flash; it rarely helps anyway.

Timing matters too. Blue hour just after sunset is best for pandal exteriors, and after about 1 am the interiors are quieter. Ask before you photograph people, and never block the aarti or a queue.

slides.title: From rajbari to sarbojanin: pujo's story
slides.sub: How a family puja became a whole city's festival

photo.artist: Louis-Henri de Rudder / After Alexei Dmitriyevich Saltykov

slides.title: Devotion, and a show of wealth
slides.body: The big autumn puja took shape among Bengal's landholding elite. For a zamindar or raja it was devotion, but also a display of wealth and standing: feasts for the poor, music and dance, invitations to the powerful.

slides.title: 1757, the year of Plassey
slides.body: Raja Nabakrishna Deb's puja is traditionally dated to 1757 and widely said to have had Robert Clive among its guests. The details come from tradition and later writers, not a precise record.

slides.line: Old family houses still hold many of the most traditional pujas

slides.title: The puja of twelve friends
slides.body: At Guptipara, it is said, twelve friends kept out of a household puja pooled money for their own, around 1790. Baro, twelve; yaar, friends. Historians treat both with caution, but the idea changed everything.

slides.title: A puja for everyone
slides.body: In the early twentieth century came pujas run by neighbourhood committees and open to all, regardless of caste or class. In the 1920s and 1930s some became gathering places for the freedom movement.

slides.title: Rajbari or theme pandal: your pick?

caption.en:
A short history of Kolkata Durga Puja, from rajbari courtyards to sarbojanin streets 📜

First came the household pujas of rajas and zamindars. Sovabazar Rajbari's, traditionally dated to 1757, is the most famous early one in Kolkata. Then came barowari pujas, paid for by groups of neighbours and traced to Guptipara around 1790. And in the early twentieth century, the sarbojanin puja: open to everyone.

Theme pandals turned it into a public art festival from the 1990s onwards. UNESCO listed Durga Puja in Kolkata in December 2021. We'd read the early dates as traditionally cited, since many come from family tradition.

Old family puja or theme pandal, where does your heart sit? Tell us in the comments 👇
